items.title: Opening credits and TEDx intro
items.description: The video opens with a transcript credit showing the transcriber and reviewer, accompanied by an on‑screen note that the event is an independently organized TEDx event.

items.title: Stallman introduces free software concept
items.description: Richard Stallman speaks on stage, stating that free software is the first battle for cyberspace liberation and asks who controls the computer.

items.title: Stallman questions computer control
items.description: He continues asking who really controls the computer, suggesting it could be a big company, and asks what a computer is.

items.title: Defining a computer as universal machine
items.description: Stallman explains that a computer is a universal machine that executes any computation given by a program, fetching and carrying out instructions.

items.title: Programs give computers instructions
items.description: He describes how a program provides instructions that the computer follows, enabling it to perform any task when the right program is written.

items.title: Stallman warns about hidden instruction sources
items.description: Stallman notes that although a computer seems to follow user commands, it may actually be executing instructions imposed by a company, limiting user control.

items.title: Two possibilities: user control vs program control
items.description: He explains that software either empowers users or subjugates them, with no middle ground.

items.title: Stallman introduces the four essential freedoms
items.description: He states that for users to control a program they must have the four essential freedoms, which are shown on screen.

items.title: Defining free software
items.description: Richard Stallman explains the four essential freedoms, distinguishes free software from gratis, and introduces the term Libre.

items.title: Freedom zero explained
items.description: Stallman states that freedom zero is the right to run a program for any purpose.

items.title: Freedom one introduced
items.description: He defines freedom one as the ability to study and modify source code, then asks what source code is.

items.title: Source vs executable
items.description: Stallman describes source code as readable text and executable as unreadable numbers.

items.title: Need source to modify
items.description: He argues that without source code, studying and changing a program is extremely hard.

items.title: Individual control via source
items.description: Stallman says having source lets each user copy and modify software for personal use.

items.title: Collective control needed
items.description: He states that non‑programmers also need collective control to adapt software.

items.title: Group adaptation of software
items.description: Stallman explains that groups can collaborate, with programmers implementing changes for the group’s needs.

items.title: Stallman explains freedom to use software
items.description: Richard Stallman says others can use the software any way they wish, emphasizing the freedom to run it for any purpose.

items.title: Stallman defines Freedom 2: redistribute copies
items.description: He explains that freedom two allows users to redistribute exact copies of the software, showing on‑screen text 'Freedom 2' and 'Redistribute it'.

items.title: Stallman defines Freedom 3: redistribute modified versions
items.description: He states freedom three lets users share modified copies, with on‑screen text 'Freedom 3', 'Redistribute' and 'with changes'.

items.title: Users control vs program controls
items.description: The speaker explains that with all freedoms users control the software; lacking any freedom lets the program and developer control users.

items.title: Proprietary software as unjust power
items.description: The speaker argues that non‑free software gives developers unjust power over users, labeling it proprietary and calling for its removal.

items.title: Proprietary software can snoop users
items.description: The speaker says proprietary software may spy on users, citing Amazon as an example shown on screen.

items.title: Stallman warns of software tracking and deletion
items.description: He notes proprietary software can snoop, track, restrict, and remotely delete books, laughing as he shows a 'FORBIDDEN' slide.

items.title: Examples of harmful upgrades and deletions
items.description: He cites Amazon deleting Orwell's book and Sony forcing PS3 upgrades that disable functionality, shown on screen.

items.title: Sony forced software change
items.description: Stallman explains that Sony can forcibly change software remotely, as illustrated by a PS3 warning screen.

items.title: Microsoft back door and NSA
items.description: Stallman says Microsoft can change Windows remotely and shares bugs with the NSA to attack users.

items.title: Proprietary software power abuse
items.description: Stallman describes how proprietary software owners exploit power to insert malicious features, not out of sadism.

items.title: Profit from user power
items.description: Stallman says companies exploit software power for profit, not malice, citing on‑screen store prompts.

items.title: Conferences on user exploitation
items.description: Stallman notes firms hold conferences to share tactics for exploiting users via proprietary software power.

items.title: Software for suckers
items.description: Stallman labels proprietary software as malware and calls it 'software for suckers'.

items.title: Join the free world
items.description: Stallman invites listeners to join the free software movement instead of abandoning computers.

items.title: Announcing GNU OS
items.description: Stallman recalls his 1983 announcement to create a free operating system named GNU.

items.title: GNU almost complete, Linux fills kernel
items.description: Richard Stallman explains that GNU was nearly complete in 1992, lacking only a kernel, which Linus Torvalds provided by releasing Linux, creating the first full GNU/Linux system.

items.title: Many GNU/Linux variants called distributions
items.description: Stallman notes that GNU/Linux has over a thousand variants, known as distributions, and warns that freedom is not guaranteed.

items.title: Most distros add non‑free software for convenience
items.description: Stallman says most GNU/Linux distributions include non‑free software for convenience, urging users to verify which distros are fully free.

items.title: Freedom requires small sacrifices
items.description: Stallman argues that preserving freedom may need sacrifices, citing Lexington as an example of a big sacrifice, but notes most are small and manageable.

items.title: To stay free, avoid non‑free applications
items.description: Stallman says wanting freedom may require giving up non‑free applications and accepting inconveniences.

items.title: Block non‑free JavaScript with LibreJS
items.description: Stallman warns that websites send non‑free JavaScript to browsers and recommends installing LibreJS to block it.

items.title: Cloud computing hides what servers do
items.description: Stallman describes how servers offer to compute your data in the cloud, hiding the process from users.

items.title: Service as a software substitute removes control
items.description: Stallman urges users to examine cloud services, which act as software substitutes that relinquish computing control.

items.title: Stallman stresses freeing personal computers
items.description: Richard Stallman argues that while many web servers run free software, personal computers should be freed first.

items.title: Stallman calls for advancing user freedom
items.description: Stallman says personal computers and people deserve freedom, calling for progress toward that goal.

items.title: Stallman identifies corporate control as obstacle
items.description: Stallman describes big companies profiting from user control as an obstacle to advancing free software.

items.title: Stallman critiques media's open source framing
items.description: Stallman criticizes mainstream media for using "open source" to avoid discussing the ethical issues of free software.

items.title: Stallman contrasts freedom vs. better quality
items.description: Stallman contrasts free software activists' ethical stance with open source advocates' focus on practical improvements.

items.title: Stallman urges talking about freedom
items.description: Stallman insists that preserving freedom requires discussing freedom itself, not just practical benefits.

items.title: Stallman likens non‑free software to tobacco
items.description: Stallman urges saying "free software" and criticizes schools teaching non‑free software as akin to encouraging tobacco use.

items.title: Stallman advocates free software in schools
items.description: Stallman argues schools should teach free software to foster independent, cooperative citizens in a free society.

items.title: Free vs nonfree software learning
items.description: Stallman explains that studying free software lets students understand how it works, while nonfree software hides its knowledge, preventing learning.

items.title: Education requires free software
items.description: He argues schools must use free software to uphold the spirit of education and hints at an even more important reason.

items.title: Sharing source code like cookies
items.description: Stallman says sharing programs in class should be like sharing cookies, requiring source code sharing so others can learn.

items.title: Share source code for learning
items.description: He reiterates that sharing source code enables other people to learn from the program.

items.title: Only free software in class
items.description: Stallman states students should bring only free software to class, except for reverse engineering, to set a good example.

items.title: Hardware secrecy blocks free software
items.description: He notes manufacturers withhold hardware information, making it shocking that they sell products without telling users how to use them.

items.title: Reverse engineering hidden hardware
items.description: Stallman explains users must study binary code to understand hardware when manufacturers refuse to share usage details.

items.title: Document hardware for free software
items.description: He urges examining binaries and documenting hardware so others can write free programs to operate it.

items.title: Human rights interdependence
items.description: Stallman says each new activity can bring new human rights that depend on each other, and losing one makes it harder to maintain the others.

items.title: Free software as human right
items.description: Stallman argues that because computing is important in society, the freedoms of free software are among the human rights that must be protected.

items.title: Protecting free software rights
items.description: Stallman states that society must establish and protect the freedoms of free software and asks how to help.

items.title: Ways to support free software
items.description: Stallman lists actions: writing free software, organizing campaigns, persuading schools and governments to adopt free software, helping users install or use it, and spreading its philosophical ideas.

items.title: Free software and Internet freedoms
items.description: Stallman says moving to free software is the first step in liberating cyberspace, but also stresses the need for network neutrality and an end to general surveillance.

items.title: Audience applause
items.description: Applause is heard as Stallman finishes his point about software and Internet freedoms.

items.title: TEDx info screen
items.description: The screen shows text encouraging viewers to visit the TEDx website for more information.
